articles.title: Wyze’s new solar-powered pan-and-tilt security camera is less than $80
articles.summary: Wyze’s new Solar Cam Pan can track and follow people moving across your property and record them in 2K.
articles.body: Wyze has announced its first battery-powered, solar-charged, 2K security camera that can rotate and tilt, providing coverage of your entire yard. The Wyze Solar Cam Pan is available now through Wyze’s online store for $79.98, making it cheaper than competitors’ offerings like Reolink’s $88 2K pan-and-tilt security camera, Tapo’s $170 4K VistaCam 360 that launched earlier this year, and the $160 3K Eufy Security SoloCam S340. Wyze says the Solar Cam Pan’s high-efficiency solar panel can keep it running continuously with just an hour of exposure to sunlight each day. The company hasn’t shared details about how long it will run on battery power alone should the weather turn cloudy for a while, or how much battery life will be reduced if the 360-degree pan, 70-degree tilt mechanism is used extensively. The camera can be controlled remotely using Wyze’s mobile app, but it also leverages AI to detect people and move the camera automatically to track their movements across your property. The Solar Cam Pan can record at night using an IR light to illuminate subjects in low-light conditions, and it can double as a deterrent to chase people and animals away using a small motion-activated LED spotlight and a siren. But it’s not designed to be used as a floodlight. [Image: The camera’s solar panel can be deatched and installed nearby to maximize its exposure to the sun. The Solar Cam Pan comes with an IP65 water resistance rating, which means you’re not limited to installing it where it’s protected against the elements. It supports two-way audio using the Wyze mobile app and offers smart home integrations with Amazon Alexa, Google Assistant, and IFTTT. Continuous local recording is an option but you’ll probably want to upgrade the camera’s internal storage using an optional microSD card up to 512GB in size. You can also connect the Solar Cam Pan to Wyze’s cloud storage with subscription plans that range in price from $2.99 per month to $19.99 per month — if you’re comfortable using the company’s connected features. Last year Wyze had a serious security breach that affected thousands of customers following vulnerabilities in now-discontinued products that the company hadn’t disclosed for years. Wyze has since been working to improve its security practices to regain the trust of consumers.

articles.title: America’s cybersecurity defenses are cracking
articles.summary: Cuts and politicization of the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) are making it more difficult for some stakeholders to rely on it.
articles.body: It was late June, and something strange was happening on Arizona’s online portal for political candidates. Images of the candidates were disappearing. Photos of the Iranian Ayatollah Ruhollah Khomeini were popping up in their place. The state would later come to believe it was an attack from an Iranian government-affiliated group. When they first discovered the threat, though, they were in the dark — and they needed help. Arizona Secretary of State Adrian Fontes’ office took action to contain the threat, which he says did not impact personal voter information. But one thing he didn’t do was contact the federal agency that would have once been among Fontes’ first calls: the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA). CISA, housed within the Department of Homeland Security (DHS), is America’s central coordinator of cybersecurity information. The agency helps organizations that run critical infrastructure ranging from elections to sanitation prepare for cyber and physical threats, and helps streamline the response to attacks when they arise. --- Are you a current or former CISA employee, or do you work for a critical infrastructure organization? Reach out securely and anonymously with tips from a non-work device to Lauren Feiner via Signal at laurenfeiner.64. --- But since the beginning of President Donald Trump’s term, CISA has faced mass staffing cuts, reassignments to immigration-related work, and recent furloughs induced by the ongoing government shutdown. The Trump administration has requested CISA’s $3 billion budget be slashed by nearly half a billion dollars and cut a reported third of its workforce. While some of this mirrors actions at other government agencies, Republicans have a special animus toward CISA, thanks to its role in tracking disinformation around the 2020 election. Now, with the agency greatly diminished and under Trump’s control, people who once worked for and collaborated with it are losing faith. Normally, Fontes would have been in regular contact with CISA, even before the attack. The agency has helped Arizona create emergency preparedness workshops for Election Day threats. Its staff would physically inspect election-related buildings, offering recommendations to make them more secure. When Arizona’s polling locations received bomb threats during the 2024 election, Fontes tells The Verge in an interview, the state got intel on the situation “instantaneously” from CISA and only had to delay one polling location by 20 minutes. “We were prepared mostly by the help of folks like CISA, and they would grease the skids between all of the other federal organizations,” Fontes says. The same should have been true for the Iran-linked hack. But under Trump, Fontes says, many of the CISA staffers his office regularly worked with have left, while Trump loyalists have taken up key posts at DHS. Its election integrity team is led by right-wing activist Heather Honey, who has promoted conspiracy theories about voting fraud. “How can I reveal security information that’s very sensitive in nature, that could be very easily exploited for political means, with an agency that’s been gutted and politicized?” Fontes says. “It would be foolish of me to do that.” Fontes says that after discovering the candidate portal attack, his office contacted the National Guard and Arizona’s Counter Terrorism Information Center, which has contact with federal agencies — but he excluded CISA as much as possible. The decision underscores how much trust the agency has lost. It also reveals a disconcerting threat to America’s cyber defenses. CISA’s value comes from its bird’s-eye view of cybersecurity. It can centralize intelligence about threats and provide recommendations based on them, along with helping less sophisticated players with training and preparation. And the agency deals with far more than elections. It focuses on critical infrastructure like water and transit systems, which experts have warned for years could be vulnerable to cyberattacks. When Microsoft Exchange Online was breached in 2023 by what the US determined to be China-affiliated hackers, “CISA was a central point for information sharing” across federal agencies and looked for other compromised areas, according to a report detailing the response. But that capability only holds up if businesses, state-level agencies, and other organizations feel like disclosing information is secure and worthwhile. The warier groups are of working with CISA, the more everyone is left at risk. It’s not just Fontes who’s worried. Earlier this year, DHS moved to disband a public-private partnership that gave utilities legal cover to share more sensitive security information with the government. Cynthia Lane, general manager of a Colorado-based water and sanitation utility, says that move raised concern about who at the federal level would push security information down to state and local stakeholders. Between the gutting of CISA staff and the government shutdown, Lane says, “it’s hard to find what the new level of activity and engagement’s going to be because there’s been so much turmoil over the last six months.” Meanwhile, people who do still contact the agency will find it harder to reach. Layoffs last month impacted nearly all 95 of the agency’s Stakeholder Engagement Division (SED) employees, which coordinate discussion with infrastructure operators, nonprofits, academic institutions, and international partners, Cybersecurity Dive reported. Compounding the problems, a law incentivizing companies to share cyber threat information by providing legal protections recently expired, and amid the government shutdown, grants for state and local governments to beef up their cyber defenses have lapsed. A three- to four-month “hiccup” in staffing up is normal at the start of an administration, says retired Rear Adm. Mark Montgomery, senior director of the Foundation for Defense of Democracies Center on Cyber and Technology Innovation. “But instead what we’ve seen is a significant stalling in the progress of improving cybersecurity across the federal government, and in some cases, backsliding.” The cuts include “key areas that could afford no losses,” he says, including the Joint Cyber Defense Collaborative, which helps improve threat information sharing between the public and private sectors. The Trump administration has denied CISA is having problems. CISA’s executive assistant director Nick Andersen said in September that despite “an awful lot of reporting recently about CISA and the potential for degraded operational capabilities … nothing can be further from the truth.” Montgomery says that assessment “defies a 250-year history of the government. We do not do these kinds of cuts and everything’s fine.” CISA’s director of public affairs Marci McCarthy says in a statement that during the Trump administration, the agency “continues to execute on its mission amid a record-breaking Democrat-led government shutdown,” and collaborates with federal agencies and private sector players to improve cybersecurity. “CISA will not operate as it did during the Biden Administration, when it inappropriately focused on electioneering and censorship,” McCarthy says. But a former CISA official, who declined to be named due to privacy concerns, warns that the Trump administration is “playing with fire” by diminishing CISA’s services. Over the past few years the US has faced several significant attacks, including a breach of Microsoft Sharepoint and a major attack on US telecom systems, which prompted officials last year to recommend all Americans use encrypted communications. “It’s only a matter of time until something significant happens,” they told The Verge. For a utility like Lane’s with 15 people on staff, CISA continues to provide free weekly threat assessments to identify weaknesses in its defenses, which it would otherwise not be able to afford. The consequence of a hack to its operational systems could be extremely tangible to the community: water main breaks caused by ramping up on the pressure on the distribution systems, or sewer overflows into nearby rivers. Fontes, for his part, was forced to weigh placing trust in CISA against the threat of losing trust from his own constituents. It’s taken years of consistent effort to build up voter confidence in how the state runs elections, and now he worries that all it could take is a Truth Social post from DHS Secretary Kristi Noem to set it on fire. “I have to look at the data that we have and the information that we have as if somebody in the administration is going to flip it over and use it against me and my administration because I’m a Democrat,” Fontes says. Fontes says the state kept DHS abreast of the candidate portal breach to the extent required by the law (without detailing exactly how). But he says his office has figured out how to keep the agency at arm’s length — what he refers to as “silent mode.” “We figured out ways to comply with the law, but also not be vulnerable to the politicized environment that CISA now presents,” he says. “The new MO is, share with who you can trust, in as limited a way as you have to to get the job done.” That might even mean withholding the kinds of minor details that only a centralized force like CISA could make sense of. “This idea of an open line of communication, where you’re sharing all kinds of stuff, even unnecessary stuff because it might connect the dots to some other things — that doesn’t exist anymore,” he says. Correction, November 10th: An earlier version of this article misstated the Trump administration’s budget cut request for CISA. It is nearly half a billion dollars, not half a million.

articles.title: Europe sent its gold to the U.S. for safekeeping during World War II. Central banks are now reshuffling their reserves for a new era of uncertainty
articles.summary: “Central banks are increasingly optimizing across three considerations: custody risk, physical accessibility, and market liquidity.”
articles.body:
Last month's announcement from the Dutch central bank that it was moving gold from North America to Europe added to the trend of a global redistribution of reserves.

The New York Fed has long served as the custodian of the gold on behalf of the U.S. government, foreign governments, other central banks, and official international organizations. Much of it arrived during and after World War II as countries sought to keep their gold reserves in a safe location.

The stockpile reached a high in the early 1970s but began a gradual slide after the U.S. took the dollar off the gold standard and is now about half of its peak.

U.S. custodianship continues to decline. France removed all of its gold from the New York Fed between July 2025 and January 2026.

Then the Dutch central bank, known as the De Nederlandsche Bank (DNB), moved more than 78 tons of gold in New York and seven tons in Canada to London, citing "increasing geopolitical unrest" and the need to improve its "crisis preparedness."

The bank's governor pointed out that London's status as the world's largest trading hub for bullion means gold stored at the Bank of England would be more accessible.

"We expect that we will never need to use them, but we do need to strengthen our resilience and preparedness," Olaf Sleijpen said.

Despite rising global tensions recently, central banks around the world have been reshuffling their gold holdings for years while also adding to their holdings.

Germany transferred 930 tons from London to Frankfurt in 2000, then sent 674 tons from New York and Paris to Frankfurt between 2013 and 2017, according to the World Gold Council .

The Netherlands shifted 122.5 tons from New York to Amsterdam in 2014, and Austria repatriated 90 tons from London between 2015 and 2018.

Outside Europe, Venezuela repatriated 160 tons from 2011 to 2012, while India has accelerated the pace of relocation since 2023.

Krishan Gopaul, a senior analyst at the World Gold Council, explained in a blog post last month that gold movements have come in waves and started well before relocation was a geopolitical issue. But the current wave is more complex.

"Heightened geopolitical uncertainty has increased attention on jurisdiction, access during a crisis, and exposure to overseas financial infrastructure," he said. "Yet recent operations by France and DNB show that the answer does not necessarily lie in domestic storage alone. Central banks are increasingly optimizing across three considerations: custody risk, physical accessibility, and market liquidity."

articles.title: Dívida de IPTU de R$ 50 mil leva ao bloqueio de pensões de idosa em MS | G1
articles.standfirst: Advogado tributarista explica em quais situações aposentadorias e pensões podem ser bloqueadas pela Justiça.
articles.summary: Advogado tributarista explica em quais situações aposentadorias e pensões podem ser bloqueadas pela Justiça.
articles.body:
Uma dívida de Imposto sobre a Propriedade Predial e Territorial Urbana (IPTU) de cerca de R$ 50 mil levou ao bloqueio judicial dos valores recebidos pela aposentada Alexandra Duarte, de 85 anos, em Campo Grande . Sem acesso ao dinheiro das pensões, ela relata dificuldades para comprar medicamentos e realizar exames médicos.

Alexandra depende dos dois benefícios que recebe para pagar as despesas do dia a dia e custear os cuidados com a saúde. Segundo a família, ao tentar sacar o dinheiro referente ao mês, a aposentada descobriu que os valores estavam bloqueados.

De acordo com a filha, Alessandra Rodrigues, o bloqueio está relacionado a uma dívida de IPTU referente ao imóvel onde a família mora.

"Fomos lá na prefeitura pra ver, aí ele falou assim 'sim, está bloqueado judicialmente. Pra gente poder parcelar, tem que pagar 300 reais', mas como que a gente vai pagar 300 reais quando o dinheiro já está bloqueado? E de onde que a gente vai tirar esse dinheiro pra poder pagar?", afirma a filha.

Além das despesas básicas, Alexandra faz tratamento de um tumor no olho esquerdo. Sem acesso ao dinheiro, ela conta que não conseguiu realizar uma ressonância magnética que já estava agendada.

Aposentadorias e pensões podem ser bloqueadas?

A cobrança de uma dívida de IPTU pode chegar à Justiça por meio de uma execução fiscal. Quando o débito não é pago nem garantido, o juiz pode determinar a penhora de bens e o bloqueio de valores em contas bancárias. No entanto, quando o dinheiro é proveniente de aposentadorias ou pensões, existem regras específicas para a penhora.

Segundo o advogado tributarista Sebastião Rolon, o Código de Processo Civil prevê a impenhorabilidade de valores provenientes de aposentadorias e pensões, ressalvadas as exceções previstas em lei. A proteção, porém, pode exigir que o beneficiário comprove a origem dos recursos bloqueados.

"Quando isso acontece, cabe ao devedor trazer aos autos as provas que efetivamente aquele valor é de aposentadoria, que o valor é oriundo de uma pensão e que, portanto, seria impenhorável ou há uma orientação jurisprudencial de que pode efetivamente haver penhora de parcela desses valores, mas sempre respeitando o mínimo existencial, a dignidade desse contribuinte."

Quem teve valores bloqueados e depende desse dinheiro para custear as despesas básicas deve procurar um advogado ou a Defensoria Pública. Extratos bancários e comprovantes do INSS podem ajudar a demonstrar que os recursos são provenientes de aposentadoria ou pensão. Com esses documentos, é possível solicitar à Justiça a análise do bloqueio e, conforme o caso, a liberação dos valores.

Como agir diante do bloqueio e evitar novas cobranças judiciais

Segundo Rolon, quando o bloqueio ocorre por ordem judicial, o contribuinte deve buscar orientação jurídica para avaliar as medidas cabíveis no processo. A instituição financeira não pode desfazer a restrição por conta própria e deve informar que o bloqueio foi determinado judicialmente.

"Efetivamente, o que resolve é ingressar no processo, analisar os autos, o grau de defesa, se for o caso pagar, realizar no parcelamento, realizar a defesa, cada caso deve ser avaliado da sua própria forma."

Para evitar que uma dívida chegue à Justiça, o contribuinte deve conferir os valores cobrados na guia do IPTU e contestar eventuais divergências. Quem tem débitos em aberto pode procurar a prefeitura para negociar o pagamento e verificar as opções de parcelamento disponíveis.

Em nota, a Prefeitura de Campo Grande informou que o ajuizamento de execuções fiscais para cobrar dívidas, como IPTU, ISSQN, ITBI e multas, segue a legislação vigente. Após tentativas de cobrança administrativa, o contribuinte tem cinco dias para quitar o débito ou garantir a execução. Caso contrário, a Justiça pode determinar a penhora de bens e o bloqueio de valores em contas bancárias.

Para regularizar as dívidas, os contribuintes podem procurar a Central de Atendimento ao Cidadão, na Rua Marechal Rondon, nº 2.655, Centro, para consultar valores, parcelamentos e descontos disponíveis pelo REFIS. A administração municipal afirmou ainda que respeita as garantias legais dos contribuintes, inclusive a proteção de valores impenhoráveis. Veja a nota na íntegra abaixo.

"A Prefeitura de Campo Grande esclarece que o ajuizamento de execuções fiscais para cobrança de débitos tributários, como IPTU, ISSQN e ITBI, e não tributários, como multas, constitui procedimento legal destinado à recuperação de créditos públicos.

Nos processos de execução fiscal, o contribuinte é citado para, no prazo de cinco dias, quitar o débito ou garantir a execução. Na ausência de pagamento ou garantia, poderão ser determinadas medidas judiciais de penhora de bens, com prioridade para ativos financeiros, inclusive bloqueios bancários por meio do sistema SISBAJUD, mediante ordem judicial.

Os procedimentos seguem a Lei Federal nº 6.830/1980 (Lei de Execução Fiscal) e demais normas aplicáveis, respeitando as garantias legais dos contribuintes. Os bloqueios decorrem de decisões judiciais no âmbito de processos de cobrança de créditos municipais, após tentativas de cobrança administrativa.

Para regularização dos débitos, os contribuintes podem procurar a Central de Atendimento ao Cidadão, na Rua Marechal Rondon, nº 2.655, Centro, onde poderão consultar valores, condições de pagamento, parcelamento e eventuais descontos previstos no REFIS.

A Prefeitura reafirma seu compromisso com a legalidade, a transparência e o respeito aos direitos dos cidadãos, inclusive quanto à análise de valores protegidos por lei."

articles.title: Musk says he will give SpaceX share to every child in US
articles.summary: Tech mogul Elon Musk said Monday he will give every child in the U.S. one share of SpaceX next year. “This will be the first of many,” Musk wrote in a post on the social platform X, which he also owns and is technically part of SpaceX. He did not specify how he plans to…
articles.body:
Tech mogul Elon Musk said Monday he will give every child in the U.S. one share of SpaceX next year.

“This will be the first of many,” Musk wrote in a post on the social platform X, which he also owns and is technically part of SpaceX.

He did not specify how he plans to go about providing shares in the company, which went public earlier this summer in the biggest initial public offering on record. However, Trump Accounts , the administration’s investment accounts for children, now allow for stock donations.

SpaceX President Gwynne Shotwell previously announced in July that she and her husband were planning to donate stock in the company to Trump Accounts for more than 2 million children, specifically teens who live in lower-income areas near the couple’s home in central Texas.

In late September, the Internal Revenue Service put forward regulations allowing for such stock contributions, suggesting it “will facilitate more donations from eligible donors, and will help create a practical pathway for large-scale private giving.”

The administration said earlier this month that nearly 8 million children already had accounts through the program. It planned to add more than 60 million others through its new auto-enrollment feature .

Kids born between 2025 and 2028 can receive $1,000 in seed money from the Treasury Department. Others can receive funds through a $6.25 billion donation from Dell CEO Michael Dell and his wife, Susan Dell. Their contribution is intended for children who live in ZIP codes with a median family income of $150,000 or less.

articles.title: Major European mobile carriers are teaming up for a ‘direct’ satellite program without Starlink
articles.summary: Deutsche Telekom, Orange, Telefónica, and Vodafone are combining forces to back a European competitor for direct-to-device satellite services.
articles.body: Deutsche Telekom, Orange, Telefónica, and Vodafone signed a letter of intent saying they’re considering a joint bid for spectrum that would support European direct-to-device satellite competition for SpaceX’s Starlink. The four telecom companies say they would handle the ground infrastructure while a separate, unannounced satellite partner provides the satellite constellation: > The joint initiative by Deutsche Telekom, Orange, Telefónica and Vodafone has a clear ambition: to meet customer demand for universal coverage in underserved areas, strengthen the resilience of public networks, protect critical communications, and support the development of a European constellation. > As part of the project, the four operators plan to establish key ground network infrastructure as well as critical coordination and monitoring functions in Europe, without investing directly in a satellite constellation. This will be provided by a satellite partner still to be selected. > The partnership between the MNO-led initiative and the satellite operator would combine European governance and market access with proven satellite technology and deployment expertise. AT&T, T-Mobile, and Verizon announced their own collaboration in the US earlier this year that would combine spectrum in rural areas and dead zones “to increase capacity, improve the customer experience, and help satellite providers reach more customers through a unified platform.” In May, the EU said it was considering a plan to reserve some of the 2 GHz band for local companies to offer satellite services, an idea that SpaceX has criticized, claiming it would worsen service in Ukraine, reports FT.

articles.title: JB Pritzker thinks AI could help us live to 100 — or threaten us like nukes
articles.summary: Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker discusses political realignment, how often to update privacy laws, why people oppose Flock cameras, and existential threats.
articles.body: Today, I’m talking with Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker, who has a lot of thoughts about AI, tech, and privacy. If you’ve been listening to the show, you know that one of my running theories is that those issues are driving a big and maybe kind of unexpected political realignment — and with the midterms coming up next month, and early voting already underway in a lot of places, the stakes are pretty high right now. So I asked Gov. Pritzker about all that, and he was surprisingly willing to dive right into the absolute existential weeds of what government is even for. You’ll hear him say — and it’s hard to disagree — that some problems are just collective action problems that require the government to do a lot of work. We can’t solve all these problems one at a time, or even one state at a time. It’s a pretty deep conversation, and we really got into it on a lot of issues. And of course, I had to ask him: Are the Bears gonna stay in Illinois? Before we get going, do me a favor and subscribe to Decoder on YouTube, where we put out new episodes every Monday and Thursday. Okay: Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker. Here we go. Gov. JB Pritzker, you’re the governor of Illinois. Welcome to Decoder. Thanks, Nilay. Great to be with you. I am very excited to talk to you. We’re in the heart of midterm season. You are running for reelection. I have to tell you. I have to be very honest with you. I personally feel a lot of pressure in this interview, not only because I’m speaking to a governor, but because I went to school in Chicago. My sister still lives in Chicago. My wife grew up in Illinois. Her entire family is farmers in North Central Illinois. Boy, do I have a list of questions for you. I have to do a good job here. Well, we’re claiming you. Now that I know all that, we’re claiming you. You’re an Illinoisan. --- [Image: Verge subscribers, don’t forget you get exclusive access to ad-free Decoder wherever you get your podcasts. Head here. Not a subscriber? You can sign up here. --- I don’t know about that. I grew up in Wisconsin. Here’s my first question for you. I’m a die-hard Packers fan. Are you going to let the Bears move to Indiana? That is not our intention. We are, in fact, in discussions with the Bears and the NFL about keeping the Bears either in Chicago or in Arlington Heights, but in Illinois. I’m saying, as a Packers fan, nothing is funnier than the outcome of the Bears moving to Indiana. I just want to put that out there. Openly biased in this case — I own two shares of that stock — but I’m going to make the comparison here. And the reason I started there is not only because I think that’s a funny outcome, although I do, but it feels like we are in the middle of a generational political realignment. I’m sure you feel that, in this election campaign, the idea of big business and how that should interact with the government, and how the government should be able to push back on big business and not give in to big business. All of that feels up for grabs. And the comparison I will make in this specific case is your fellow governor, Gavin Newsom, in California. They sued the Ellison family, Paramount, over the Warner Brothers merger. Paramount threatened to leave. They made a lot of noise about Nashville, Texas, Miami, or wherever you make noise about these days, and it feels like Newsom caved. It feels like he pressured his Attorney General, Rob Bonta, to settle that lawsuit and keep them there. They settled the lawsuit. The next day, the Ellison family is like, “We never... We’re from California. We would never leave.” I see a parallel here with the Bears that is connected to that larger realignment, how government and business should interact. Do you see that parallel? Do you feel that realignment? Well, what I can tell you is we’re pretty tough negotiators in Chicago and Illinois, and that’s really what we’re in the midst of now with the Bears. But I understand your point about realignment. I mean, there is a generational change, and I think it’s also an attitudinal change about protecting taxpayers, protecting people who frankly are among the most vulnerable to all the technology that’s overtaking people’s lives and invading people’s homes. And so I do believe that the government has to be more active now and become a fighter for our people and not just a collaborator with business on everything. I’m a businessman, as you know, before I became governor. But I also know that, for the people of Illinois anyway, my job is to protect the working people of this state who often don’t have anybody protecting them except a government that will stand up for them. So that’s kind of the realignment that I see. And that generational shift, I agree with you. It’s partly a Democratic Party generational shift. Generationally, we’re a little more aggressive. And I’m probably older than the next generation that’s already possibly taking office this November. I’m 61 years old, but I think of myself as having come out of the tech world and as somebody who has been a fighter for progressive values that, yeah, we’ve got to become more aggressive and make sure we’re standing up for our people. There are two places where I see the realignment in particular. One is data centers, one is privacy, and you just see that as a bipartisan backlash to those things. I would actually add a third, which is antitrust broadly. It’s weird if you go into Silicon Valley. David Sacks is retweeting Lina Khan from the Biden administration talking about whether the AI industry needs an antitrust exemption to manage safety. They both agree that these companies don’t need antitrust exemptions. They actually should be more competitive. Again, putting that in the context of regulating these companies, thinking about the dynamic between the government and the biggest companies in the world. I’ll just ask the question, I guess, more directly. Do you think Newsom was right to give in to Paramount, or do you think he should have forced them to make good on that threat to leave? I can’t speak to the Paramount situation well enough to give you an answer, so it would be unfair for me to do so. I can say once again that our orientation today — and I think about the big AI companies and the big social media companies as well — has to be like, wait a minute, too much power in too few hands. Particularly when we talk about AI, where it’s potentially existential, but certainly transformative, which is probably a kind way to say it about the economy, that we’re going to have to get very engaged. Guardrails, of course, on both parts, but also addressing what I think on the AI front is potentially a significant change in employment in the United States. I’m not somebody who is necessarily convinced that we have to see a whole bunch of job loss, but that does feel like that’s the direction this is going. And part of that is a generational shift that’s needed and a better understanding. We have people who are serving in the United States Senate who have no idea. Was it the Secretary of Education, Trump’s Secretary of Education, who called it A1? I mean, because we’ve got older people who don’t have any exposure who are making policy theoretically on these things, and it should disturb us all. It’s one of the reasons we’ve got to advance the cause of better people and better systems in government. We are on the cusp of an election. There might be a new Congress. There might be new leadership in Congress. There are a bunch of old Democrats too. In fact, I could probably point directly to Joe Biden’s age in the last election as the reason that he lost. Do you think that you need a wholesale change of leadership of the older Democrats as well? You said, “Do we need a wholesale change?” I mean, I can tell you that I don’t think we should be telling — Well, now I live in New York. I’ll just ask you, do you think Chuck Schumer should be the Senate majority leader if the Democrats take the Senate? That’s a decision people in the Senate are going to make. I have no influence over it. I can tell you this: I am opposed to term limits because I think that you should have all the choices. You’re a voter. If you want to vote for the 75-year-old, I mean, go ahead. I’m just suggesting that a great case could be made for the 45-year-old who’s just as smart as the 75-year-old was when he was 45, or maybe is now, but has a modern look at the issues around AI privacy, everything else we’re discussing, and a more aggressive view of how we ought to be reining in big corporations in their invasion of our lives. But I think people ought to make their own choices. I mean, for us to say, “Well, we should have an age limit. You’re 70, that’s it, you’re out.” I think that belies who we are as a democracy. Well, you convinced me. I’m 46. I’m announcing my run for president here with you, Governor. That was a rousing speech. Listen, I would vote for you in a second if the choice was you and Donald Trump. A low bar, but I’m glad I crossed it. Let me tie two ideas together at the end. We’ve talked a lot about AI regulation. You mentioned social media regulation a little bit earlier in this conversation. I know that Illinois has a social media law. You have a bell-to-bell ban on phones in schools for kids. I’m just going to pick on Mark Zuckerberg. It’s easy to pick on Mark Zuckerberg. If you look at how he talks about social media regulation, he basically describes the tragedy of the commons. You signed the landmark settlement with him. I think Illinois is due to get $750 or $760 million out of that settlement. And a big part of it is that TikTok and YouTube have to agree to the same terms, and then Meta will pay the rest of the money. And Zuckerberg very clearly has said that’s because if Instagram falls back on engagement bait and TikTok doesn’t, the kids will just use TikTok. And so the government has to get everyone to agree. I will tell you that Neal Mohan, the CEO of YouTube, does not agree. He’s not going to sign onto this. That’s one whole fight. Look at how Mark Zuckerberg talks about AI regulation. There’s none of that dynamic at all. He’s like, “It should be a free-for-all. We’ll all compete. If it’s not safe, the market will tell us. We’ll be fine.” And in my mind, these ideas are at total odds with each other. In the market where he makes all the money, the government has to step in and stop him from hurting kids because apparently there’s no market demand for safe social media. And in the market where the AI CEOs are telling us they might kill us all if we don’t stop them, it’s a free-for-all, and the market will tell us if they accidentally kill everybody. How do you reconcile those things? Are you just happy that you got the social media case done after a decade of failing to regulate social media, or do you think you can solve AI with regulation this time instead of letting it just cook? Look, I’m an optimist at heart, so I’m not going to suggest to you that I absolutely know that we can solve all the problems that we’re now facing, but I don’t know what else we can do. Other than, again, progressively making sure that we’re trying to address each of these things, trying to anticipate them to the extent we can. Can we be faster than AI is developing? I don’t know. But we can’t stop trying. I know that. And I would suggest to you that my optimism is founded because I think the vast majority of people want what you’re describing, which is reining it in. And again, without destroying companies. I don’t think we’re all trying to do that. What we’re trying to do is stop the invasion into our home, stop the invasion into our children’s lives. I do think we can do that, but that’s because we’ve solved a whole lot of huge problems. That’s kind of like my answer to: is AI potentially existential? The answer, of course, is yes. And can we solve it? I don’t know. Nuclear weapons... I mean, just to give something of an analogy to something else. I mean, nuclear weapons are still hanging over us as a danger to humanity. And so far anyway, we’ve managed not to blow up the world. I don’t know whether that gives you any optimism, but it does to me. We, as a country, can figure out how we want to rein it in here. That we, as a country, can work with our allies to figure out how we want to collectively try to rein it in. And then we have enemies in the world and competitors in the world, and we’ve got to figure out how we’re going to... Maybe it’s mutually assured destruction, like it was with nuclear weapons, but these are all things we’re going to have to work on, and work on fast. And it’s scary because someone analogized this to... I mean, think about the early 1950s when every kid had to learn that if there was a nuclear blast, an atomic bomb that went off, get under your desk. That wouldn’t have been very effective. But the point is, people lived with the idea that a terrible nuclear holocaust could occur with a nuclear explosion. And so I think we’re heading into that world again with AI. I hope I didn’t stray too much from your question, but — Let me ask you this, and it’s a little bit of a wild card here at the end. We cover this industry so closely here, and the big difference with nuclear weapons is that there weren’t five companies building bleeding-edge nuclear weapons in private capacity, led by five guys who all hated each other. But that’s the dynamic of the AI industry. They all truly hate each other, and they’re all trying to make as much money as they can as fast as they can. And then some of them think the AI is alive. If you ask Anthropic, and we’ve done this, “Is Claude alive?” They don’t say no. They will argue with you about the definition of alive and suggest that, to them, alive means having a biological component and Claude doesn’t have that, but it might be conscious. There’s a race to build AGI in the industry. Some people truly believe they’re building alien minds that have a different kind of consciousness. I’m not sure any government at any level has ever had to regulate that, or has ever come up against an industry that is religious about the fact that it might be building the next kind of intelligence. Where do you stand? Do you think that they’re building a next kind of consciousness that stands alongside humans, or do you think that this is normal technology as some others do? Boy, that is really another podcast for us, but I’ll just say this one thing: I just want to disagree with you for a second. Nobody could ever imagine a nuclear weapon either. And... But the government built nuclear weapons. It wasn’t — I understand. I’m not suggesting it’s the same. I’m suggesting it’s so new at the time that figuring out how you’re going to rein it in… Because remember, it’s not just one government, and the same thing with AI. It’s not just those five guys either. I mean, it’s like there’s somebody in China. Maybe five of those. I don’t know, and somebody in Europe or whatever. You could say we’re ahead, or they’re ahead. I don’t know. But all I’m saying is, yeah, this is a proliferated situation and it’s not government-controlled. One hundred percent, you’re right; it’s not like nuclear weapons in that sense. But it is like nuclear weapons in the sense that nobody’s ever seen it before. It’s a complete mystery to start with. How are we going to rein it in? I mean, nobody thought Russia was going to get the bomb, and they got it. We’ve figured out somehow how to deal with it. Again, you’ve got to be an optimist to believe we can end up with the right solution here. I don’t know that we have the answer to “how do we rein it in?” I will say, though, that if we had the power to create it, we have the power, in my view, to rein it in. Is it conscious? You’re asking a deep question. Have you felt the AGI? I mean, do you think it’s conscious? Because I understand why people think it might have consciousness or it’s going to be conscious. But I think that’s why the ethicists and technologists need to be involved. And especially, in my view, the government’s got to be involved because how else are you going to rein in the five guys and the companies that have developed this? There is no other way. I will tell you, I don’t think it’s conscious. And every now and again, you have an experience where it’s blindingly clear why other people believe that. When you watch a reasoning model take 90 steps over an hour and arrive at a conclusion, it’s impressive, and you can see why people believe that. I do not, and I have a lot of reasons for that. It just occurs to me that if you set out to regulate a technology like this, if you believe one thing, you would maybe go down one path. And if you believe that you were building a consciousness, you might go down another. Again, the whole industry itself does not agree on this. Jensen Huang and Dario Amodei do not agree on whether it’s alive. Jensen just wants to sell a bunch of chips, and he will happily tell you it’s just technology and you can control it. I think Dario thinks he’s building AGI, and that’s a different... There’s a whole reason he proposes different kinds of regulatory structures there. I’m just asking you, have you felt the AGI? Do you think it’s one path or the other? I’m not going to give you a satisfactory yes or no. I mean, I haven’t felt it. I guess that’s what I’m... My basic answer is I haven’t felt it. Governor Pritzker, this was very fun. Thank you for indulging this last existential loop of a question. You’re going to have to come back to Decoder soon. I would like to do that. Thanks, Nilay. articles.title: Saudi Arabia postpones its 'Davos in the Desert' conference after attacks
articles.summary: By Timour Azhari, Federico Maccioni, Tala Ramadan and Alexander Cornwell Oct 19 (Reuters) - Saudi Arabia has decided to postpone its flagship investment conf...
articles.body:
By Timour Azhari, Federico Maccioni, Tala Ramadan and Alexander Cornwell

Oct 19 (Reuters) - Saudi Arabia has decided to postpone its flagship investment conference until next year, organizers confirmed in ‌a statement on Monday, following deadly attacks which rocked the kingdom in recent weeks as ‌the Middle East conflict widens, disrupting business.

The Future Investment Initiative, or FII, was planned for October 26 to 29, but ​will now take place in 2027, with a new date to be announced "very soon," the organizers said. Reuters reported earlier Monday that the in-person event had been scrapped and organizers were weighing postponing the event.

The conference, set for its 10th edition, has become a must-attend event for some of the world's top ‌financiers. Informally dubbed "Davos in the Desert," ⁠in a nod to the World Economic Forum's annual meeting in Switzerland, the state-backed annual event has showcased the kingdom's ambitious investment plans in a ⁠bid to attract billions of dollars needed to fund its economic transformation away from hydrocarbons towards tourism, sports and technology.

Expected speakers for this year's event included Goldman Sachs CEO and Chairman David Solomon, Standard Chartered ​CEO ​Bill Winters and Citi's CEO Jane Fraser, according to ​a draft programme.

The US-Israeli war with Iran ‌this year has disrupted the Gulf's busy calendar of events, with several conferences cancelled, postponed or retooled in the UAE and Qatar in the first part of the year, when the countries bore the brunt of the attacks while Saudi Arabia suffered fewer hits.

The kingdom in recent weeks has faced an escalating war with Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthis, which have struck military, energy and civilian infrastructure across the country, ‌including state oil company Aramco's headquarters and Riyadh's international ​airport, where strikes killed at least 18 people and ​hundreds were wounded this month.

FII said it ​wanted to ensure the event delivered "the full scale, extraordinary quality, and unforgettable impact ‌that our community has come to expect."

Reuters ​reported last week that ​the FII organizers considered a hybrid format, allowing executives to tune in remotely. Semafor reported Monday that big banks and private-equity firms have privately relayed safety concerns about attending the event ​to Saudi Arabia's Public Investment ‌Fund Governor Yasir Al-Rumayyan, adding that CEOs feel pressure to attend the four-day event.

(Reporting ​by Timour Azhari, Federico Maccioni, Tala Ramadan and Alexander Cornwell. Editing by Anousha Sakoui, ​Elisa Martinuzzi, Maha El Dahan and Tomasz Janowski)

articles.title: Burgum: East Potomac will be transformed into ‘best course in America’ under Trump
articles.summary: Interior Secretary Doug Burgum argued a major renovation of East Potomac Park and its public golf courses is a necessary move by the federal government, as President Trump’s plans to redevelop the land face an intensifying legal challenge. “I mean, there are examples of this around the country, famous golf courses, which golfers would know,”…
articles.body:
Interior Secretary Doug Burgum argued a major renovation of East Potomac Park and its public golf courses is a necessary move by the federal government, as President Trump’s plans to redevelop the land face an intensifying legal challenge.

“I mean, there are examples of this around the country, famous golf courses, which golfers would know,” Burgum said Monday during an appearance on Fox News, comparing the president’s vision to major championship venues like Torrey Pines in Southern California and Bethpage State Park on Long Island.

“And all of these are courses that hold national tournaments and have international claim. But they’re publicly owned courses with low prices for the people that live in that immediate area, which is what we would do here,” the Interior secretary continued, arguing a priority of the administration is “maintaining that public golf.”

Trump has eyed the property at Hains Point in central Washington, D.C., for months and over the weekend posted a graphic showing plans for an 18-hole championship length course designed by leading golf course architect Tom Fazio.

For years, East Potomac has been home to one 18-hole course and two shorter courses catering to younger and beginner golfers, plus a driving range and clubhouse.

The park is also used daily by thousands of bikers, walkers and joggers who use paths that would be eliminated as part of the president’s plans.

Trump’s announcement over the weekend came after hundreds of trees — including cherry trees that bring thousands of tourists to D.C. every year — were removed from the property in recent days despite a court order halting work there.

The government’s redevelopment plan is facing a legal challenge from local preservationist groups and D.C. golfers who argue the president is illegally carrying out work on federal public land. East Potomac is part of the National Park System.

“But right now … we’ve taken out already two miles of broken-down fence. We’ve got the seawall around the wall, and the thing is like the tidal basin,” Burgum said during his appearance on Fox.

“And it is a, you know, the trees, there’s pictures of Harding and Coolidge and others that were — and Taft — golfing on this course in the early 19, the teens and the 20s when this course was made. And there was barely a tree on the course. All of its presidents. And it’s the Washington Monument in the background.”

“So doing some getting rid of some of these hazardous trees is restoring it back to its historical nature when this course was made,” the secretary continued. “But it’s a public course. It could be the best course in America with the lowest prices. That’s the intention of the National Park Service. And we’re looking forward to getting going on that.”

Trump has repeatedly said he does not need approval to begin on the project next month, and attacked U.S. District Judge Ana Reyes directly, calling her “insane” for admonishing government attorneys over the work done being at East Potomac while the case is being litigated.

The pipeline project was scrapped in…
articles.body:
The Trump administration is giving a defense-related boost to a contentious pipeline in the Northeast U.S.

The Energy Department said Monday that it would give up to $42 million from the Defense Production Act for the Constitution Pipeline project that would transport natural gas from Pennsylvania to New York.

The pipeline project was scrapped in 2020 after New York officials denied it a key approval.

However, Williams Companies expressed renewed interest in the project last year after apparent support from the Trump administration.

Last year, the Trump administration also said it would allow an offshore wind project to move forward after New York Gov. Kathy Hochul (D) made “comments about her willingness to move forward on critical pipeline capacity.”

At the time, Hochul’s office denied that there was a deal on any natural gas pipelines.

On Monday, the Trump administration said that its funding would support pre-construction and permitting activities needed to advance the project, and after it receives permits, could support the deployment of gas infrastructure.

“President Trump promised to lower energy costs and reverse the energy emergency he inherited that was caused by 17 years of energy subtraction policies. That is why he promised to build the Constitution Pipeline — a project that will transform the lives and economic opportunities for Americans across New York and New England,” Energy Secretary Chris Wright said in a statement.

Meanwhile, a spokesperson for Hochul criticized Monday’s announcement.

“Today’s announcement is nothing more than a political ploy to divert attention from Trump’s tariffs and his reckless war in Iran that have not only failed to bring down prices as the President promised, but have dramatically driven up home energy costs and gas prices at the pump,” said Ken Lovett, Hochul’s senior communications adviser on energy and environment, in a statement.

“While the President continues to obsess over blocking renewable energy projects in order to focus on gas, oil and even coal, Governor Hochul is focused on driving an all-of-the-above energy strategy designed to keep the lights on and costs down for New Yorkers,” Lovett said.

The Defense Production Act was passed during the Korean War as an effort to help the government jumpstart industries needed for defense purposes.

articles.title: DHS orders removal of DeepSeek from government agency IT systems
articles.summary: The Department of Homeland Security (DHS) has ordered that products from the Chinese AI startup DeepSeek be removed from federal agency IT systems and barred from government contracting. The order, which initially went out in July, was published on the Federal Register website Monday. It said DeepSeek’s AI models present “multiple threat vectors,” noting the…
articles.body:
The Department of Homeland Security (DHS) has ordered that products from the Chinese AI startup DeepSeek be removed from federal agency IT systems and barred from government contracting.

The order, which initially went out in July, was published on the Federal Register website Monday. It said DeepSeek’s AI models present “multiple threat vectors,” noting the Chinese government has “extensive authority” to access private infrastructure.

DHS warned that the models can collect personally identifiable information and may “track or digitally fingerprint” users, in addition to potentially containing malware or other security vulnerabilities.

The prompt-and-response process in some of DeepSeek’s most widely used applications could result in the “transfer of sensitive data to the PRC [People’s Republic of China] if used by U.S. government or vendors,” the agency added.

“The transfer of the aforementioned information to the PRC, either independently or in combination with publicly available data, could produce actionable intelligence on U.S. persons and/or government programs,” the order said.

DeepSeek sent shockwaves through Washington and Silicon Valley last year when it released its R1 model.

It drew comparisons to top American models from OpenAI and Google but was developed with reduced capacity chips and at a fraction of the cost, raising fears that China was gaining on the U.S. amid fierce competition between the two superpowers.

articles.body:
Extração ilegal de minérios é descoberta em Paraty — Foto: Divulgação/Disque Denúncia

Uma extração ilegal de minérios foi descoberta na segunda-feira (19) após denúncias em Paraty (RJ). O caso aconteceu durante a “Operação Protetor dos Biomas 2026”.

Agentes do Linha Verde, que é um programa do Disque Denúncia voltado para o meio ambiente, foram até a Rodovia Rio-Santos (BR-101), na altura do km 83 e, constataram a extração irregular de uma substância mineral, conhecida como saibro e é utilizado em obras de pavimentação, preparação de terrenos, fundações e argamassas.

De acordo com Disque Denúncia, no endereço, foram encontradas marcas de máquinas escavadeiras em uma área degradada de cerca de 1.200 m². Ninguém foi preso.

Ainda segundo o Disque Denúncia, o flagrante configura crimes ambientais previstos no Código Florestal e no decreto SELCA.

O caso foi registrado na delegacia de Paraty, que está responsável pelas investigações. O Disque Denúncia informa que para denunciar crimes ambientais, a população pode ligar para o telefone (21) 2253-1177 e para o 0300 253 1177 .

He’s pitched his lot in with the dictator and the war criminal, and he’s being harsh and undermining the democracy, the country that wants to be part of the West, part of the EU, would love to be part of NATO, would love to be allied with us,” Bacon said in an interview with CNN’s Jake Tapper, discussing both Russian President Vladimir Putin and Ukraine, respectively.

“Putin hates us. The president doesn’t see that. But to say that Russia’s been fine on Ukraine and they bomb cities every night, I was there a month ago. They’re bombing gas stations, restaurants, shopping malls. They’re committing terrorism against Ukrainians,” he added.

On Monday, Trump said he had not yet agreed to a trilateral meeting with Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping, but said he was open to it.

“I would do it,” Trump told reporters on the White House’s South Lawn. “Not so much on Ukraine because Russia, frankly, has been fine on Ukraine, they haven’t been doing much, and the same with China.”

“We would have it to talk about weapons and denuclearization,” he added.

The president’s comments followed reporting from The Wall Street Journal that Putin proposed a trilateral meeting to talk about the war in Ukraine during a call with Trump earlier this month.

Last week, Trump went after Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky, claiming he was “not a good guy for us to deal with.”

During a Newsmax interview, the president was asked about Ukraine restarting attacks against Russian energy targets following Trump asking Zelensky to halt such strikes.

“Zelensky is not a good guy for us to deal with,” the president said. “I’m not a big fan of Zelensky. They’ve destroyed that country.”

“If they’re going to end up with a settlement of some kind, they’re not going to do it with” Zelensky, Trump said when asked if he backed additional military aid for Ukraine.

The Federal Reserve's latest message could reach well beyond Wall Street — straight into your credit card statement and, for some homeowners, the monthly bill that keeps a roof over your head.

Buried in the minutes (1) of its September meeting, released Oct. 7, was a sentence borrowers have reason to pay attention to:

Jeff Bezos backs a platform that lets anyone invest in rental homes for as little as $100 — 6 ways to build wealth like a landlord without actually being one

Gold has overtaken U.S. Treasuries as central banks' top reserve asset. Get Priority Gold's 2026 Precious Metals IRA Playbook for free

"Most participants assessed that another increase in the target range for the federal funds rate would likely be appropriate by year end."

That follows the Fed's September decision to raise its benchmark rate by a quarter percentage point to a range of 3.75% to 4%.

Fed Chair Kevin Warsh underscored the concern at his September press conference (2): "The plain fact is that inflation is too high, and has been for too long."

For households already juggling expensive groceries, utilities and debt payments, the message is sobering: some bills could climb further.

America has approximately 3.1 million active adjustable-rate mortgages, according to Intercontinental Exchange (3). These loans can change rates after an initial fixed period, potentially leaving homeowners with larger payments. Not all face an immediate adjustment, but knowing your reset date matters.

Credit card borrowers face a similar squeeze: variable rates can rise with the benchmark they follow, making outstanding balances more expensive to carry.

The Fed's next decision arrives Oct. 28, but you don't have to wait to examine your options.

If you have an adjustable-rate mortgage (ARM), start with the date your current rate stops being fixed. Check when your rate next adjusts and when the first payment at the new rate would be due. Ask your mortgage servicer for two estimates: your expected new payment and the highest payment permitted at that adjustment.

An ARM's rate generally follows a benchmark index plus a lender-set margin, subject to caps on how much it can change. Your loan's terms determine when — and how sharply — your payment can move.

Put the estimates into your household budget. If the numbers don't work, exploring refinancing early gives you time to compare alternatives. Weigh the new rate, closing costs and repayment term; a lower monthly payment isn't always a cheaper loan overall.

articles.title: No wonder the White House wants Warsh to cut: A 1% Fed rate hike costs the Treasury an extra $95 billion a year in national debt interest
articles.summary: “Even if primary deficits remain largely unchanged, the growing interest burden materially increases the government’s financing needs,” the analysts wrote.
articles.body:
There are many reasons—none particularly surprising—that politicians and policymakers push central banks for a lower base interest rate. It makes borrowing cheaper and stimulates the economy, potentially leading to more jobs and home purchases. It also, conveniently, makes the government's own borrowing costs cheaper. While leaders the world over have lobbied for lower base rates for these reasons, none have done it quite so forcefully as President Donald Trump and his team. First, they went to extraordinary lengths—including personal insults and a criminal investigation—against previous Fed chairman Jerome Powell, and now the broader Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) led by new chairman Kevin Warsh.

Trump and his team have suggested that rates are too high, hurting consumers' chances of owning a home as a result (mortgage rates are tied to long-dated rates). But Bank of America has also put a figure on the cost to the government of elevated interest rates.

"Clients are concerned about U.S. fiscal deficit risks. We are too," wrote BofA analysts Meghan Swiber, Stephen Juneau, Mark Cabana, and Ralph Axel. "Higher rates become increasingly costly the longer they persist. The near-term deficit outlook has changed little, but the rates backdrop has changed the longer-run fiscal math.

"Higher yields compound into materially greater interest expense and Treasury financing needs over time, while raising the risk that the eﬀective interest rate on the debt eventually exceeds nominal growth. Debt spiral starts when interest costs exceed nominal growth."

Treasury payments to service the $40 trillion national debt surpassed $2 trillion for the 2026 fiscal year, the department recently announced.

In a recent analysis , the Congressional Budget Office (CBO) forecast the alterations to projected service payments on the debt under two interest rate scenarios. In the first, rates were 150 basis points higher than current projections between 2026 and 2036, and in the second, rates were just 50 basis points higher.

In the first scenario, in which interest rates are 1.5% higher than forecasts, deficits are $6 trillion larger, with a $4.9 trillion increase in net interest costs. A 0.5% increase results in $1.9 trillion added to current debt projections, with an extra $1.6 trillion added in net interest costs.

"Even if primary deficits remain largely unchanged, the growing interest burden materially increases the government's financing needs," the analysts wrote.

"We estimate that interest expense rises $95 billion a year for every 100bps of Fed hikes," the team wrote.

articles.title: TikTok employees said they knew about child safety issues, but execs failed to act
articles.summary: TikTok was repeatedly warned by its own staffers about risks its platform posed to child safety
articles.body: TikTok was repeatedly warned by its own staffers about risks its platform posed to child safety, according to court records obtained by NPR. The publication reports that employees were frustrated over TikTok executives failing to appropriately act on concerns they raised, including minors bypassing age-restricted content, and appearing in “transactional sexual content” the company could financially benefit from. The previously unreported depositions of TikTok staffers were filed in federal court in March, and connected to a multi-district litigation initiated in 2022 that brings together hundreds of lawsuits alleging that TikTok, Meta, Snap, and Google knew that they social media platforms are harmful to children, and failed to disclose those risks. One deposition from Reagen Maher, who held senior safety and investigations positions between 2021 and 2024, described flagging the prevalence of “transactional sexual content” to then-TikTok CEO V Pappas, regarding minors stripping on TikTok’s Live feature in exchange for “gifts” that can be converted into real currency. Forbes reported on the issue in 2022, and Maher said the company was already aware of the sexual exploitation concerns before the article was published. “I have been fighting about fixing this for months with people who didn’t think the harms are severe enough,” Maher said in an excerpt from an internal chat with a colleague. “Put simply, senior leaders know about this issue. There are some ongoing projects to fix parts of it, and frankly, I’m hoping [that] this article puts a fire behind other potential solutions.” Another deposition from TikTok’s former head of safety Eric Han says he was concerned about harmful algorithm “rabbit holes” in 2020, describing them as having a “real contagion effect” regarding “suicidal ideation and behavior” in an internal TikTok report. Despite flagging that “minor safety is an urgent issue that we must address effectively,” Han said that TikTok failed to warn parents of the potential dangers of their child using the platform.

articles.title: Beijing monitoring US warship near disputed shoal in South China Sea
articles.summary: China on Tuesday accused the U.S. military of “illegally” entering waters around a disputed shoal in the South China Sea, saying it had sent its own forces to watch a Navy ship. China has claimed roughly 90 percent of the South China Sea as its own territory, leading to disputes with the Philippines, Malaysia, Vietnam…
articles.body:
China on Tuesday accused the U.S. military of “illegally” entering waters around a disputed shoal in the South China Sea, saying it had sent its own forces to watch a Navy ship.

China has claimed roughly 90 percent of the South China Sea as its own territory, leading to disputes with the Philippines, Malaysia, Vietnam and other Indo-Pacific nations.

To demonstrate the vital shipping and economic corridor is not under Beijing’s sole control, the U.S. has sailed its warships through the area in so-called “freedom of navigation operations.” The last such known mission in the South China Sea took place more than a year ago.

But the Chinese military asserted that in the early hours of Tuesday, the USS Charleston littoral combat ship “illegally intruded” into waters adjacent to Sabina Shoal in the Spratly Islands without approval from the Chinese government, according to a statement.

China’s Southern Theater Command Navy “dispatched forces to track and monitor the U.S. vessel in accordance with laws and regulations,” it said.

“The U.S. action infringes upon China’s sovereign rights and interests, jeopardizes maritime security, and is detrimental to regional peace and stability,” China said in the statement, which demands that Washington “should immediately cease such activities.”

The Pentagon and Navy did not immediately respond to a request for comment from The Hill.

A Philippines’ military spokesperson, however, told Reuters that the U.S. ship “did not trespass into ‘Chinese territory’,” and that no nation had the authority to need prior permission for “lawful transit through international waters.”

Tensions between China and the Philippines remain constant over a disagreement as to the sovereignty of Sabina Shoal and the Spratly Islands archipelago.

The two nations were involved in an altercation last month when a Chinese Coast Guard ship rammed a Philippine boat near Sabina Shoal, the Philippine Coast Guard claims. China disputes the account, blaming the Philippines for the collision.

articles.title: Philadelphia Eagles face backlash for handling of Jalen Hurts blood clotting issue
articles.summary: The Philadelphia Eagles are facing intensifying criticism for how the team handled a major health complication involving its star quarterback, who the Eagles announced will miss the rest of the season due to a potentially fatal blood clotting condition. Hurts, who won a Super Bowl MVP award with the Eagles in 2025, initially suffered a…
articles.body:
The Philadelphia Eagles are facing intensifying criticism for how the team handled a major health complication involving its star quarterback, who the Eagles announced will miss the rest of the season due to a potentially fatal blood clotting condition.

Hurts, who won a Super Bowl MVP award with the Eagles in 2025, initially suffered a calf injury during a game against the Los Angeles Rams on Oct. 4.

After telling Eagles staff about the injury during a practice the following week, Hurts traveled to London where the team was slated to play the Jaguars that Sunday.

Hurts was seen by a specialist in London who diagnosed him with a left calf superficial vein thrombosis, according to the Associated Press, and Hurts was allowed to play against Jacksonville and fly home to the U.S. afterward.

Hurts was notably kept awake for 36 hours before the London game, reportedly for fear sleep could worsen his condition.

The Eagles signal caller threw for 220 yards and a touchdown in Philadelphia’s 19-17 loss to the Jaguars that day.

In a statement on Monday, Hurts’s agent said the star quarterback underwent extensive testing once he returned to the United States that revealed a more serious blood clotting issue in his lungs that will require blood thinners to treat.

A number of medical experts have posted a steady stream of videos on social media in the hours since explaining it is extremely dangerous for athletes to play contact sports while taking blood thinners given the high risk of internal bleeding, particularly in the head.

Eagles coach Nick Sirianni deflected questions from reporters on Monday about why Hurts was allowed to play against Jacksonville and fly home with the team despite his condition.

“I’m not a medical expert,” Sirianni said. “I lean on our guys in all those situations. I’m a football coach. I lean on our medical experts in every situation. I have full trust and full faith in them. It’s not just me that has major care for our players. It’s them, as well.”

The Eagles handling of Hurts condition is being met with widespread condemnation from the club’s fans and sports medicine experts.

“The Eagles have a lot of questions to answer,” said the former ESPN anchor and sports media pundit Trey Wingo in a video posted to social media.

“The Eagles are scared as hell because they might have cost this kid his life and could have cost him his damn career,” said former NFL tight end and commentator Shannon Sharpe during a recent episode of his podcast.

“Jalen Hurts is a friend of mine and I’ve got a ton of respect for him, so his health should be the most important part of this conversation,” said analyst Marcus Spears on ESPN’s Monday Night Countdown. “But I want to know how did Jalen Hurts get from a superficial blood clot in his leg to blood clots in his lungs and played a football game in between and flew over to London in that time.”

Hurts is currently on a five-year deal with the Eagles worth more than $200 million, including nearly $180 million in guaranteed money.

articles.title: Former OpenAI worker accused of bugging conference room planned travel to Saudi Arabia: Prosecutors
articles.summary: A former OpenAI employee accused of bugging the company’s offices was planning to leave the U.S. for Saudi Arabia when he was arrested earlier this month, according to federal prosecutors. Abdulrahman Alfozan, a 35-year-old Saudi national who worked as an engineer at OpenAI, was arrested in early October for allegedly hiding a recording device in…
articles.body:
A former OpenAI employee accused of bugging the company’s offices was planning to leave the U.S. for Saudi Arabia when he was arrested earlier this month, according to federal prosecutors.

Abdulrahman Alfozan, a 35-year-old Saudi national who worked as an engineer at OpenAI, was arrested in early October for allegedly hiding a recording device in the AI firm’s San Francisco offices.

In a court filing Sunday, prosecutors argued Alfozan should be detained pending trial, suggesting he “has little incentive to remain in the United States to see this case through.”

They underscored the former OpenAI engineer has “considerable resources and ties to Saudi Arabia” and “was mere days away from leaving the United States for Saudi Arabia when he was arrested.”

Alfozan initially planned to fly to Riyadh with his wife and son on a one-way plane ticket on Oct. 12. After he was arrested on Oct. 9, his wife and son left the country the next day on a one-way plane ticket to Doha, Qatar, booked and paid for by a Saudi military official, according to the filing.

“The day before she left the United States, the defendant’s wife told the FBI agents who interviewed her that her U.S. visa was expiring and that she and her son were permanently moving back to Saudi Arabia—and that her husband, the defendant, eventually intended to do the same,” prosecutors said.

He was also in “frequent communication” with a member of the Saudi royal family, who was trying to recruit him to work on a Saudi AI initiative, and had applied to a program based in Riyadh, according to the filing.

However, Alfozan’s lawyers argued for pretrial release in a filing Friday, noting “his entire adult life” is in the U.S. and he was “weeks away” from an interview for his citizenship application.

His upcoming flight to Saudi Arabia was booked several weeks before the recording device was found and Alfozan was arrested, they added.

“If his intention was to flee, he would have done so at that time,” his lawyers wrote. “The October 12 departure date was fixed by federal immigration rules: it is the last day of the sixty-day grace period his wife was permitted to remain in the United States after her post-completion work authorization ended.”

They also suggested the one-way nature of Alfozan’s ticket was not abnormal, as he typically purchased one-way tickets and booked his return later.

A recording device was discovered in an executive conference room at OpenAI’s offices in late September, where it was plugged into a USB port on the back of a television and covered in toilet paper.

Alfozan was arrested shortly after, with prosecutors pointing to video surveillance footage showing him near the conference room in the days before the device was found and appearing to peer behind the television where it was placed about a week later.

Another recording device was found in his bag, while other similar electronic components were found at his home, prosecutors said. A chatbot used by his wife also showed inquiries about continuous audio recording, live listening and speech-triggered recording.

articles.title: China defends DeepSeek after US ban
articles.summary: China is pushing back against the Department of Homeland Security’s (DHS) order to remove products from Chinese AI startup DeepSeek from government systems, warning of potential retaliation. A DHS order, which dates back to July but published to the Federal Register Monday, said DeepSeek’s AI models present “multiple threat vectors,” and ordered them to be…
articles.body:
China is pushing back against the Department of Homeland Security’s (DHS) order to remove products from Chinese AI startup DeepSeek from government systems, warning of potential retaliation.

A DHS order, which dates back to July but published to the Federal Register Monday, said DeepSeek’s AI models present “multiple threat vectors,” and ordered them to be removed from federal agency AI systems and barred from government contracting.

When asked on Tuesday about the order, Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesperson Mao Ning said Beijing “consistently opposes overstretching the concept of national security and politicizing tech and trade issues.”

“We will resolutely safeguard Chinese businesses’ lawful rights and interests,” she told reporters at the briefing in Beijing.

DHS warned DeepSeek’s models can collect personally identifiable information and may “track or digitally fingerprint” users, along with containing malware or other security vulnerabilities.

The prompt-and-response process in some of DeepSeek’s most widely used applications could result in the “transfer of sensitive data to the PRC [People’s Republic of China] if used by U.S. government or vendors,” the agency said.

The Associated Press later reported China’s Ministry of Commerce expressed “strong dissatisfaction and firm opposition” against the order, arguing the U.S. disregarded the agreement reached between Chinese President Xi Jinping and President Trump.

Under “the guise of national security,” the U.S. is attempting to suppress China, the commerce ministry said, the AP reported. “China will closely monitor the situation and take all necessary measures to firmly defend its legitimate rights and interests.”

DeepSeek’s models stirred up anxiety in Silicon Valley and Wall Street at the beginning of last year when it released the R1 model, which drew comparisons to U.S.-made models for a fraction of the cost.

During Xi’s visit to Washington, D.C., last month, the two world leaders discussed AI , which Trump has taken to calling super intelligence.

The U.S. and China agreed to launch new talks on AI and establish a channel for handling AI-related incidents. The first AI-specific talk is scheduled for November.

Competition between China and the U.S. on AI development remains tight as Beijing pours its resources in open-source models, which are cheaper, but often less secure. DeepSeek has both open-source and proprietary models, which are available around the world, including in the U.S .

articles.summary: Google is launching a new browser safety feature for Chrome that aims to keep you better informed about how malicious a website might be before you open it.
articles.body: Google is launching a new browser safety feature for Chrome that aims to keep you better informed about how malicious a website might be before you open it. The new suspicious site warnings, available when Chrome’s Enhanced Protection is on, build on a similar two-stage system introduced for Chrome file downloads in 2024, which provides visually different notifications for blocked files based on whether they’re determined to be “suspicious” or “dangerous.” For the Chrome site warnings, the feature will flag a website as suspicious if it detects that it has similar qualities to other sites associated with phishing, malware, and scams. Google describes this warning as having a “lower confidence verdict” with possible risk of user harm — meaning there’s a chance it could be incorrectly flagged, but you should only proceed to the site if you’re 100 percent confident that it’s safe to do so. The warnings on “dangerous” website have a higher confidence verdict and “high risk of user harm,” however, and should be avoided entirely. It’s easy to distinguish between these warnings at a glance. The notifications for suspicious websites will appear as a pop-up window on both desktop and mobile, with the webpage visible but darkened underneath, and an option to “Mark as safe” if the site was flagged mistakenly. The already familiar notification for dangerous sites is much harder to ignore: the warning message takes up almost the entire screen and the website will be replaced with a solid red background. Google also improved Gemini-powered scam detection for Enhanced Protection users, alongside introducing the browser warning redesign.
