articles.body:
President Trump on Tuesday posted a series of photos showing crews removing trees from East Potomac Park , insulting the peninsula that he is seeking to redevelop starting next month.

“Here are pictures of Trash Island for the Judge to study,” Trump wrote in his Truth Social post. “This is just a small area, and better than some!”

The president was making reference to U.S. District Judge Ana Reyes, who earlier this fall ruled to halt work that was being carried out by the National Park Service while a preservationist group and local D.C. golfers sue to stop Trump’s plans.

The NPS cut down hundreds of trees at the property earlier this year in what administration officials have said was an effort to restore the course to its original links style design.

The president is seeking to close East Potomac Golf Links, D.C.’s most widely used public golf facility, and revamp it into an 18-hole championship-length facility designed by renowned golf architect Tom Fazio.

Under the National Links Trust, which operated the courses until this year, East Potomac became known for its affordability in an area that is home to some of the country’s priciest and most exclusive private clubs.

East Potomac Park, in addition to being home to three golf courses, is used daily by thousands of bikers, walkers and joggers who would lose access to the property as part of Trump’s plans.

Trump has repeatedly said the East Potomac property is “dangerous,” and play should not continue there, posting a design for a new course on Truth Social over the weekend and saying work would begin on Nov. 15.

It is unclear when the photos the president posted on Tuesday were taken, but a recent order issued by Reyes forbids any future tree cutting while the case is being litigated.

Trump attacked the judge on Monday, calling her “insane,” while his allies have sought to justify the work being done there.

During a recent interview on Fox News , Interior Secretary Doug Burgum said under Trump East Potomac “could be the best course in America with the lowest prices. That’s the intention of the National Park Service.”

articles.title: Meta pauses Muse sharing after researchers find AI chats on the web
articles.summary: Meta says it’s pausing a feature that lets you share artifacts and conversations with its Muse AI assistant after security researchers found exposed AI chats on the web.
articles.body: Meta says it paused a Muse feature that lets you share conversations with the AI assistant after researchers found the URLs publicly available on the web, as reported by Ars Technica. In a report published this week, researchers at the security firm Claroc say they found more than 6,800 Muse links through public DNS records. “People have the ability to share specific Muse artifacts, which creates a page that can be accessed by those with the link,” Muse spokesperson Tracy Clayton says in an emailed statement to The Verge. “However, we’ve paused this functionality while we review this report and consider changes to how these links can be discovered.” The feature in question allows you to share your Muse conversation with someone else through a link. But, as pointed out by Claroc, the way Meta designed these links made them easy to find. “Muse builds each share’s web address from the share’s title, a short phrase describing the conversation, then a random ID,” Claroc says. “The hostname usually gave away what a page held before we opened it, and since the link carries that same title and ID, a hostname pulled from DNS rebuilds the link.” By searching public DNS records, which serve as a directory for web traffic, Claroc was able to view hundreds of Muse conversations, including some containing a marketing company’s revenue review, a small business owner’s loan application, a workplace’s full-year staff calendar, and notes for a job candidate’s call with an AI lab. This isn’t the first time AI sharing features made chats more public than intended, as conversations with OpenAI’s ChatGPT, Anthropic’s Claude, and xAI’s Grok have wound up on Google Search.

articles.title: CDC recognizes third measles death, still short of Pennsylvania count
articles.summary: The Centers for Disease Control and ​Prevention (CDC) has added a third U.S. measles death to its national tracker as total cases for 2026 surpass 4,400. The Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) told Reuters the CDC updated its count after the National Center for Health Statistics received ​a report of a measles-related death…
articles.body:
The Centers for Disease Control and ​Prevention (CDC) has added a third U.S. measles death to its national tracker as total cases for 2026 surpass 4,400.

The Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) told Reuters the CDC updated its count after the National Center for Health Statistics received ​a report of a measles-related death and verified the disease was the underlying cause, the Department of Health and Human Services said in a statement. The agency’s database does not specify when or where the death occurred.

According to the statement, the CDC is working with the Council of State and Territorial Epidemiologists to develop a standardized case definition for deaths due to measles.

“This work is intended to promote consistent classification and reporting of measles deaths across jurisdictions,” the statement said.

The addition comes shortly after the CDC announced it was sending a disease expert to Pennsylvania — the state with the largest portion of measles cases — to assist with the outbreak. But the federal agency still won’t acknowledge the full, six-person death count the commonwealth has recorded this year.

The CDC website states the number of deaths it recognizes could change as the agency updates its reporting.

Earlier this month, Pennsylvania authorities reported a sixth death connected to the largest measles outbreak the state has faced in decades. The total number of confirmed cases in the commonwealth has crossed 1,200, according to its health department .

The state health department updated its outbreak death toll after the Franklin County Coroner’s Office reported a 39-year-old woman with “several underlying conditions” died following a recent measles diagnosis.

The outbreak in Pennsylvania sparked a feud between state and federal officials. In August, Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro (D) accused the Trump administration, namely Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. , of spreading misinformation that led to declining vaccination rates.

Kennedy, who has publicly peddled theories linking vaccines to health conditions, defended himself against the governor’s accusations — saying Shapiro provided no evidence that he has spread misinformation and accusing him of politicizing the state’s outbreak.

Last week , Sen. Bill Cassidy (R-La.), chair of the Senate Health, Education, Labor and Pensions Committee, argued the Trump administration is not promoting vaccinations vigorously enough.

“My concern as a physician is that everyone should be vaccinated for measles,” Cassidy told CNN’s Jake Tapper. “And you may think it only affects me. That’s not true because you infect other people.”

About 96 percent of Americans infected with measles this year were either not vaccinated against the illness or had an unknown vaccination status, according to the CDC .

In response to the outbreaks, the CDC has issued roughly $100 million in additional funds to state, local and tribal health departments for vaccinations, prevention and disease detection efforts. Despite the funding and support, infectious diseases specialists argue a clearer messaging campaign at the federal level would help strengthen the response to the outbreak.

articles.title: Can you see everything?
articles.summary: I spent four months covering Elizabeth Holmes’ trial for fraud. You Can See Everything reveals her methodology.
articles.body: This review contains spoilers. I have heard it said that of all the drugs, fame is the most addictive. For Elizabeth Holmes, at least, I am willing to believe that is true. It is the only explanation for You Can See Everything, a movie that is, at its core, about several varieties of manipulation. Holmes, as the CEO of Theranos, was a business-world celebrity: a woman who’d built a private company valued at $9 billion around a miniaturized blood testing platform that supposedly let people test just a drop of blood for a variety of ailments. She had a deal with Walgreens, speaking gigs, a New Yorker profile, a cover story in Fortune; Fox News mogul Rupert Murdoch was among her investors and Henry Kissinger sat on Theranos’ board. The company crumbled after John Carreyrou, then a reporter for The Wall Street Journal, broke the story in 2015 that Theranos wasn’t using its own technology to run most of its blood tests. Only 15 tests were run on the Theranos machine, and insiders had doubts about their accuracy. In 2021, I spent four months sitting through Holmes’ trial for fraud. She was found guilty of one count of conspiracy and three counts of wire fraud. The evidence supporting that verdict was damning: forged memos that appeared to be from pharmaceutical companies Theranos had done testing for; recordings of Holmes lying about doing testing in Afghanistan with the American military and claiming Theranos could perform more than 1,000 tests on its proprietary machines, even though only 200 were listed as options on the website because “we have operationalized certain tasks, expecting a certain set of ordering patterns.” Several Theranos employees testified they’d told her their misgivings about the accuracy of the proprietary tests, only to be summarily dismissed. They faced harassment and retaliation as a result of talking to Carreyrou — nastygrams from Theranos lawyers, bizarre investigations from Fusion GPS, and private investigators tailing them. In one case, Holmes nearly destroyed the relationship between a man and his grandfather. (You can read the grandson’s review of the movie here.) These specifics do not appear in You Can See Everything. That isn’t its project; the film assumes you have some familiarity with the Theranos scandal. Holmes approached A24, the studio behind the film, to see if it would be willing to do a documentary; cringe comedian Nathan Fielder found out and asked if he could call her. Fielder and his team filmed Holmes’ last month of freedom, and then stayed in contact for two more years as she served her sentence. The question the film poses is: Can you trust her? This is not, if you were immersed in the details of the criminal case, a question. (No. Obviously.) What is fascinating is that Fielder got sucked in anyway. Early in the film, Fielder asks Holmes if she has chosen him to tell the story because he isn’t a science journalist, and it’ll be easier to get one over on him. She says she sees it as a human story. She feels she has been misunderstood. She isn’t the fraudster people — like me, I suppose — made her out to be. She wasn’t lying to anyone. She really believed in her invention. As she says this, she is wide-eyed, making eye contact with Fielder. Her face is placid, even peaceful. She appears to be fully convinced. At one point, she insists she’s never told a lie at all, not once in her life. It is a spectacular performance. I might even have believed some of what she was saying, if I hadn’t seen hundreds of pages of documents from her trial. At one point, she tells Fielder that when she said her machine “can” perform all those tests, she meant the machine can, if you make the hypothetical chemistry for the tests, perform the tests. A future-tense “can,” if you will. (And a somewhat tautological one.) This was not an entirely novel talking point; in fact, it was the reason that one day of the trial contained a grammar lesson. Fielder’s response was to try to take this future-tense “can” seriously, or as seriously as he can, by showing Holmes “Who’s on first,” a 1945 comedy routine by Abbott and Costello that she professes not to have heard of. (It is so famous that my first contact with it was my father doing both sides of the routine verbatim when I was perhaps five. The routine is almost 10 years older than he is.) Holmes laughs along, then when asked what’s funny, appears to draw a blank. She is seemingly unable to produce the name of the first baseman. I find it difficult to believe that a grown woman cannot comprehend a comedy routine that I understood as an ordinary five-year-old. But Holmes has to commit to not understanding it, because to admit she understands it is to admit she understands why the future-tense “can” misled people. Her partner, Billy Evans, offers that her mind doesn’t work like other people’s. This is true, in its way. One of the reasons that Fielder, a master manipulator himself, winds up so entangled in Holmes’ story is that he isn’t going to the written records. The only meaningful appearance of Theranos-era Holmes is a brief recorded clip of her talking to journalist Roger Parloff, which is what kicks off the “can” discussion. In the absence of any kind of permanent record, talking to someone who appears perfectly confident and candid while they lie is a mind-bending experience. Onscreen, Fielder wants to believe her. He doesn’t, not really. But he wants to. Later, we do see text: an iMessage from Holmes to Fielder, the line from which the title is drawn, reassuring him that he can move in with the couple. He can see everything. It is, in context, a normal use of the word “can.” Because I was not preoccupied with the same thing as onscreen Fielder — trying to figure out whether Holmes was “fully sincere” or “the most manipulative person who ever lived” — I was watching, instead, how the manipulation works. In the early shots, Fielder is lurking awkwardly in the background, or around the corner from Holmes in a shot. But Holmes draws him in, asking him what he thinks, engaging him in conversation. Holmes’ penchant for eye contact does a lot of it; at one point, Fielder asks her how she and Billy met, and whether she was flirting with him. She was. He asks how she flirts. She says, while holding eye contact with Fielder, by holding eye contact at length. Fielder and Holmes are often in very close physical proximity, which is emphasized by Lance Oppenheim’s (and Fielder’s) direction. In some scenes, they appear to be about to kiss. This is notable largely because of who Holmes operates best on: men. She was surrounded by them at Theranos — the only girl in the boys’ club. But the seduction here isn’t the femme fatale style of noir movies. It’s eye contact, active listening, physical proximity. She is giving Fielder — and, I presume, the other men in her life — the feeling of being fully heard and understood. On top of that, there’s a second level of seduction operating: the promise that you, the person she is talking to, are uniquely qualified to understand her, because you are special. One question that my court experience didn’t really answer for me was how Holmes did it. I did not find her especially compelling in her public appearances. She was good on the stand — far and away the best defendant I’ve seen testifying on their own behalf in any civil or criminal case — but not especially seductive. The film showed that she operates best one on one. Her charisma isn’t about her. Not exactly. It’s about how she makes her interlocutor feel. And she’s very good. Because when Evans tries to evoke the same thing with Fielder — suggesting to him that Holmes has been misunderstood and thus persecuted, but Fielder is special enough to see Holmes’ side of the story — Fielder sees through it. “I know what you’re feeling,” Evans says to Fielder. Fielder immediately dismisses this as an absurdity: “No, you don’t.” Evans’ relationship with Holmes is the primary focus of the last two-thirds of the documentary, and it is similarly fascinating to anyone with background knowledge about Holmes. During the Theranos years, she was in a relationship with Sunny Balwani, who was later her codefendant in the fraud trial. Holmes successfully got their trials severed by claiming her relationship with Balwani was abusive. Early in the documentary, Evans takes a bowl of eggs from Holmes to beat them more forcefully than she does, before handing it back. Holmes tells Fielder that Evans doesn’t like how she beats eggs, implying he does this a lot. Before Holmes goes to jail, Evans has her photographed to create an avatar of herself, like a hologram, that can be used to create what are, effectively, deepfakes generated from letters she might write. When Fielder raises the concern that AI deepfakes may be made of Holmes nude or in compromising positions, Evans essentially shrugs. Evans has also taken over Holmes’ X account, and is writing some distinctly non-Holmes-like posts on it. He didn’t get the password from her — he says he got it from X employees. Before Holmes goes in to be recorded for her hologram, she tells Fielder that she doesn’t like having her picture taken, and that she didn’t like all the press around Theranos. This sticks with Fielder as a concern about Evans, about the possibility that Evans is manipulating Holmes. It does not seem to trouble him that this is in complete conflict with inviting an entire film crew into your home to make a documentary about you. Holmes seems to have activated some kind of protective instinct in Fielder. But Holmes loves attention, the record shows. In the Theranos days, Balwani texted her he was worried about “overexposure,” which she immediately dismissed; she wrote to him about using the media to “drown out and refute the crap.” Holmes likes the attention and thinks she can control it. This is clear from Evans’ operation as a proxy. When Fielder starts talking to Holmes’ parents about what she was like before Evans, he interrupts and herds them away. Fielder told Wired that this was a problem throughout production: “Sometimes we’d be trying to do shoots, and Billy would be trying to stop it or just be like, ‘That’s enough time.’” Holmes’ relationship with Evans is one where Evans views himself as in control — as he is with the AI-generated imagery of Holmes and with her X account. He tells Fielder that he just knows what she would want — evoking Gaius Baltar in Battlestar Galactica, with his visions of Caprica Six — and so he doesn’t have to ask her. Fielder, understandably, finds that alarming. But Fielder himself has summoned up his own fake Holmes: Amanda Seyfried, the most sensible person in the entire documentary. Seyfried shows up both as herself — as a kind of audience stand-in for Fielder — and to reenact interactions that took place off-camera, effectively reprising her turn as Holmes in the 2022 Hulu miniseries The Dropout. Seyfried is there to reenact Holmes’ and Fielder’s off-camera interactions, particularly a confounding episode where Evans — with Holmes out of the room — demands payment for the documentary, and producers at A24 concede. Seyfried and Fielder are determined to get to what Holmes knew and when, culminating in an unfilmed encounter between Fielder and Holmes at the prison, which Seyfried acts out. Because of the time pressure, Fielder and his crew started shooting the film before there was any agreement in place. During the (off-camera) bargaining over the contract, that gave Holmes and Evans leverage to play hardball. In the reenactment of that bargaining session, Seyfried’s Holmes leaves the room; while she’s gone, an actor playing Evans asks for a cut of the documentary’s profits. The film cuts back and forth between Fielder and Seyfried’s discussion of the interaction and Seyfried’s reenactment. Did Holmes know, and deliberately step away so that Evans could ask? Or is she being taken advantage of by yet another would-be Svengali? Fielder travels to the prison, where he has an ambiguous conversation with Holmes — or at least, one that is ambiguous in his recollection. As he is telling Seyfried about it, effectively doing a table read for the scene, Seyfried immediately asks Fielder if he is protecting Holmes, if he is leaving something out. Fielder’s reply is vague. Evans at times appears unstable, especially near the end of the documentary. When he meets Seyfried, he tells her she isn’t good at social media because she made some comments around Charlie Kirk’s death — comments I had no idea she’d made because I don’t monitor Seyfried as closely as Evans apparently does. He goes on an aggressive, paranoid rant, saying that he is always armed, and that no one would like his politics. Perhaps Evans was sober as a judge, but the constant sniffing, the aggression, and the paranoia sure reminded me of conversations I’ve had with people who were fully zooted on cocaine. It is this version of Evans that claims Holmes doesn’t know he asked for a cut of the documentary proceeds. This is also when Evans says he just consults his head-Holmes to know what she would want — that the real Holmes doesn’t enter the loop. In order to operate as Holmes did at Theranos — outsourcing any conflict to a man nearby who can handle it for you — she has to make some sacrifices. Most people who are well balanced don’t want to be a human shield. This limits Holmes’ selection; the men who want to get in fights for her are men who want to get in fights, period. The men who are most likely to want to “protect” her are the ones who also will want to control her. That was the alleged downside of her arrangement with Balwani and it appears to be the downside of her relationship with Evans, too. It is also the downside of her relationship with Fielder, who has produced a documentary in which his team has the final cut. The people who will assent to being used are also the people who are likeliest to turn around and use Holmes herself. Fielder goes to the prison to talk to Holmes about whether she knew she’d get money from the film; given her history with Balwani, I assumed she’d been fully briefed by Evans about what to expect. So when she claims to have a head-Evans who talks to her so she doesn’t have to consult the real thing, I was not especially surprised. That Fielder was alarmed enough about her relationship to try to get her alone suggested to her that she needed to do some image control. The film’s post-script text reveals Evans gave up his financial stake in the documentary. The documentary itself was meant as image rehabilitation, and so the conflict of interest and its appearance in the documentary itself undercut Holmes’ image. In the end, the question Fielder is most hung up on is: Does Holmes believe everything she says? I don’t think this matters much. The film gives you the disorienting, claustrophobic experience of trying to deal with Holmes in real time, which is part of its pleasure. Holmes is a specific example, but what troubles Fielder throughout the film is part of the problem of having any relationship at all. In reality, most of the time, you cannot pause and consult written evidence, because federal prosecutors haven’t read our emails and text messages in open court. You just have to decide whether you are willing to trust someone. Exactly how far was Fielder taken in? We see the “you got this” goodbye from her as she leaves for prison. We get a reenacted scene of Holmes comforting Fielder about a breakup over the phone from prison, and a reenacted prison hug. Early in the documentary, Holmes invites Fielder for a swim in the ocean, and he says he doesn’t like cold water, and he’s not sure what breaking that boundary would mean. At the end of the film, after Seyfried asks Fielder if he is protecting Holmes, we see footage of the two of them playing in the ocean. On the one hand, it sure looks like Fielder got got. On the other hand, it’s a deliberate choice to include those scenes in that order, and it is part of what elevates the film into high art. Either Fielder is manipulating Holmes and the viewers to suggest he’s more malleable than he actually is, or Oppenheim and Fielder are including footage showing that Fielder was successfully manipulated. For the film’s directors, I have no written evidence to go to. Your guess is as good as mine.

articles.title: Why your VPN keeps triggering extra security checks
articles.summary: A dedicated VPN IP address may reduce frustrating CAPTCHAs and bank login security checks by giving websites a consistent connection to recognize.
articles.body: Ever notice that websites keep asking you to verify your identity when you're using a VPN? Whether you're checking your bank account, signing into email or shopping online, those repeated security checks can get frustrating. Your VPN may be part of the reason. A VPN changes the IP address websites see, which can sometimes trigger additional verification requests. Fortunately, a dedicated IP address may help reduce those interruptions while keeping your VPN protection enabled. Here's what you need to know. Join our upcoming CyberGuy LIVE class: 5 Ways to Travel Smarter and Save Money In this free live online class, Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson will share five practical ways to protect your trip and your wallet this holiday travel season. You’ll learn how to secure your phone and personal information, find better travel deals, avoid common scams, save money on bookings and use technology to make your travels easier and less stressful. No technical experience is needed. Join us Saturday, October 31, at 11 AM ET / 8 AM PT. Register free now at CyberGuyLive.com. YOUR BANK MAY STOP TEXTING YOU SIX-DIGIT CODES How VPNs can affect your logins First, let's set the record straight: A VPN generally does not interfere with how your passkeys or two-factor authentication codes work. Time-based authenticator codes are generated on your device and can work without an internet connection. Passkeys use cryptographic keys to verify your identity during a sign-in, while push notification approvals require a network connection. A VPN can usually work alongside all of these methods. What it does change is the public IP address websites see. When you connect through a VPN server, websites and apps see that server's IP address instead of your usual public IP address. That's the whole point. But it's also why banks, email providers, and financial apps sometimes get nervous. These services use your IP address as one of many signals to decide whether a login looks legitimate. If you always log into your bank from roughly the same location and the same address, and suddenly your account is being accessed from a different city or a different country, the system flags it. Not because your VPN broke anything, but because from the app’s point of view, someone new just walked in the door. Why changing IP addresses can trigger extra security checks One common trigger is a VPN connection that uses shared IP addresses. Your public IP address may change when you reconnect or switch servers, although some VPN connections can keep the same address across multiple sessions. For a bank or workplace login portal that recognizes your usual login patterns, an unfamiliar IP address or location can raise a red flag. The second trigger is shared IP addresses themselves. When hundreds of users connect through the same VPN server, they all appear to be coming from the same address. Websites and security systems recognize these addresses as VPN traffic and treat logins from them with extra suspicion. That means more CAPTCHAs, more verification steps, more temporary lockouts. Neither of these is a flaw in your VPN. It's doing exactly what it's supposed to do. But if you're regularly logging into sensitive accounts, those extra security checks can get frustrating fast. How a dedicated IP can reduce login interruptions One potential solution is a dedicated IP address. Instead of sharing an IP address with other VPN customers, you receive a fixed address reserved for your use. Each time you connect to that dedicated VPN location, websites see the same public IP address. This consistency may help reduce unnecessary CAPTCHAs and security checks, especially on services that consider your usual login location. However, a dedicated IP doesn't guarantee that a bank or website will recognize your connection as trusted. Security systems also evaluate your device, account activity and other risk signals. Some VPN providers offer dedicated IP addresses as part of their subscription plans or as a paid add-on. These services let you maintain a consistent IP address while keeping your internet traffic encrypted through the VPN. However, privacy protections vary by provider, so check how your dedicated IP is assigned and whether it can be linked to your account. There is also an important trade-off. Because only you use your dedicated IP, websites may find it easier to associate repeated visits with the same address. Shared VPN addresses can provide greater privacy against IP-based tracking by mixing your traffic with other users. For people who frequently encounter login interruptions, a dedicated IP may provide a more consistent browsing experience without giving up VPN encryption. For the best VPN software, see my expert review of the best VPNs for browsing the web privately on your Windows, Mac, Android and iOS devices at CyberGuy.com. ANTI-SCAM SETTINGS ON IPHONE, PIXEL AND GALAXY YOU SHOULD CHECK A few extra tips to avoid VPN login problems If you're still running into extra verification requests, here are five things worth trying. 1) Switch to a different VPN server Some VPN server IP addresses trigger more security checks than others. Try connecting to a server closer to your actual location. This may help reduce verification requests, although websites can still recognize VPN traffic. 2) Use split tunneling for trusted apps Some VPN services offer split tunneling, which lets you choose which apps use the VPN connection. For example, you might allow your banking app to connect directly to the internet while keeping other apps protected by the VPN. Just remember that apps bypassing the VPN will expose your regular public IP address. Feature availability varies by provider and device. Only bypass the VPN for sensitive apps when you're using a network you trust. 3) Check your authenticator app's clock If your six-digit authentication codes aren't working, your device's clock could be the problem. Time-based codes depend on accurate time settings. Make sure your phone's date and time are set to automatic. If codes still fail, confirm you're selecting the correct account in your authenticator app. 4) Let trusted websites remember your device Some websites offer a "Don't ask again on this device" option after you verify your identity. Selecting it can reduce repeated security checks on your personal computer or phone. Make sure your browser allows cookies for those websites, since private browsing or automatically clearing cookies can cause them to forget your device. Never use this option on a shared or public computer. 5) Don't approve unexpected login requests A VPN can trigger extra security checks, but that doesn't mean every authentication request is legitimate. If your phone asks you to approve a login you didn't initiate, deny it. Someone could be trying to access your account. Check your recent account activity for unfamiliar sign-in attempts. If you spot anything suspicious, change your password and review your account's security settings. HOW TO FIND COMPROMISED PASSWORDS ON IPHONE AND ANDROID Kurt’s key takeaways I like the extra privacy a VPN provides, but I can understand how repeated security checks could get frustrating. A VPN generally works alongside passkeys and two-factor authentication without interfering with their underlying security. However, changing IP addresses and shared VPN connections can prompt websites to request additional verification. A dedicated IP may reduce those interruptions by giving websites a more consistent connection to recognize. It won't eliminate every security check, but it can make frequent logins more convenient. The most important thing is to keep your authentication protections enabled, even when an extra verification step feels inconvenient. articles.title: Former NATO commander: ‘No balance’ to Trump decision ‘to give in to Russia’
articles.summary: Former NATO Supreme Allied Commander Wesley Clark on Monday said there was “no balance” in President Trump’s decision “to give in to Russia” after waiving sanctions and agreeing to permit Russian diesel into the U.S. while supporting Ukraine’s war against the Kremlin. “The most important thing is to maintain the rights of nations to be free…
articles.body:
Former NATO Supreme Allied Commander Wesley Clark on Monday said there was “no balance” in President Trump’s decision “to give in to Russia” after waiving sanctions and agreeing to permit Russian diesel into the U.S. while supporting Ukraine’s war against the Kremlin.

“The most important thing is to maintain the rights of nations to be free of invasion,” Clark told “Elizabeth Vargas Reports” host Elizabeth Vargas on NewsNation, The Hill’s broadcast partner. “Why would he trust [Russian President Vladimir Putin] anyway? Why would he trust Putin anyway? He shouldn’t trust Putin. I mean, why would he?”

Clark later added, “I’ve always tried to present a balanced view, but there’s no balance to this decision of the president to give in to Russia. We’ve seen it for a long time.”

The former NATO leader recounted his trip last week to Warsaw, Poland, for a security forum when he learned of Elon Musk’s Starlink services being cut off to Ukraine , leading to dozens of Russian missiles striking around the capital of Kyiv.

“They know that President Trump is not the leader of the free world,” Clark continued. “They think he’s in a corrupt bargain with Vladimir Putin. And it really works me as an American to have people say that about our president.”

Clark later added that he hopes Congress intervenes and warned that Trump’s policy toward Ukraine and Russia was “bad.”

“I hope President Trump is listening to this,” he said. “I hope President Trump will appreciate the fact that this is something he should back away from. He needs [Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky] there.”

Trump’s diesel deal and the waived sanctions stirred backlash from bipartisan lawmakers on Capitol Hill.

Lawmakers sent a letter to Trump and Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent urging them to reconsider the diesel deal and explain how the president can “reconcile” the Treasury Department’s license with an existing ban on Russian energy imports to the U.S.

House Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) on Sunday said his team and the White House “need to talk about” the waiver and “carefully consider the unintended consequences that may ensue from that.” He added that he knows the “president’s evaluating this as he does everything else.”

Zelensky slammed Trump over the deal, calling it a “ birthday gift ” to Putin, and advised the U.S. not to make a “ historic mistake ” by offering Putin support. He has advocated for negotiating an end to the conflict, with the support of the U.S. and European allies, a goal that administration officials agree with. Trump has said a settlement must be reached first.

The Ukrainian president also resumed strikes on Russian refineries following a brief energy ceasefire announced by Trump earlier this month. He said he felt betrayed by the U.S. as Russia continued its attacks on Ukraine despite the ceasefire’s implementation.

Trump blasted Zelensky in an interview with Newsmax last week as “not a good guy for us to deal with” and said he was “not a big fan” of the Ukrainian leader.

articles.title: Hegseth says Ukraine posture unchanged, but ‘our guys’ need interceptors too
articles.summary: Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth said on Tuesday that the U.S. government’s posture toward Ukraine is unchanged, but emphasized that “our guys” need Patriot missiles interceptors too. “There’s a lot of things that have been said in the press that are not true about the Department of War,” Hegseth told reporters in Eau Claire, Wisc. when…
articles.body:
Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth said on Tuesday that the U.S. government’s posture toward Ukraine is unchanged, but emphasized that “our guys” need Patriot missiles interceptors too.

“There’s a lot of things that have been said in the press that are not true about the Department of War,” Hegseth told reporters in Eau Claire, Wisc. when asked about reports of the Pentagon holding up some Patriot missile interceptor transfer from Kyiv allies.

“We haven’t changed our posture in any way toward the Ukrainians, but certainly with things like interceptors, we want to make sure our guys have the most possible as well,” Hegseth said.

The Ukrainian military relies on Patriot interceptors to shoot down Russian drones and missiles that have been lighting up Ukrainian cities since the full-scale invasion began in 2022.

Hegseth remarks come following reports that the U.S. was holding up the delivery of the weapons systems to Ukraine.

President Trump has been feuding with Ukraine President Volodymyr Zelensky while suggesting the fault for the war lies more with Ukraine and Zelensky than Russian President Vladimir Putin.

Trump over the last two weeks signed a deal allow Russia to export diesel fuel to the U.S., and then waived sanctions on Russia put into place by recently approved legislation named for the late Sen. Lindsey Graham (R-S.C.).

“Well, as the president has said, Ukraine’s had a heroic effort, and there’s been a great deal of contributions,” Hegseth said Tuesday. “In fact, so much so under the previous administration that they emptied stockpiles that the president is making sure we refill. That’s part of the arsenal of freedom, and not only are we not refilling, we’re going even further with those stockpiles.

“So that’s and President Zelensky knows that we’ve had very earnest conversations with him about it, but I think what Marco said, what the Secretary of State said about that, is spot on,” Hegseth said, referring to Sec. of State Marco Rubio.

“Our policy hasn’t changed. Ultimately, the President does want to see peace. He believes that the killing should stop. It’s it’s not necessary that it need to continue, and he wants both sides to come together on that.“

Trump on Tuesday at a news event in the Oval Office again called for the war to end, noting the high number of casualties on both sides.

articles.title: Trump bets existing laws can police AI. Will they be enough?

articles.body:
The Trump administration is taking the position that existing criminal and civil laws will be enough to hold artificial intelligence developers accountable in an age of unpredictable AI agents, even as legal experts question whether this will be enough.

President Trump’s so-called “ Super Intelligence (SI) Force ” argues it can create standards for AI firms with laws already on the books under the Justice Department and Federal Trade Commission (FTC).

But there is no clear consensus among the legal and tech community on whether these laws will sufficiently manage the risks posed by AI, or as Trump refers to it, super intelligence.

“People want action now because there is very real harm happening now,” Chinmayi Sharma, an associate law professor focused on AI, cybersecurity and internet governance at Fordham University, told The Hill.

“I don’t think there is consensus, or that we necessarily know enough, or have thought through this really complicated issue enough to be able to confidently say these are exactly the laws that are needed to do what we want to do,” she added.

The legal questions surrounding AI have come into sharp focus in the wake of a series of recent cybersecurity incidents.

Agents from OpenAI hacked into the tech startup Hugging Face and an Australian government health website in recent months, while agents from Anthropic submitted a false homicide tip to the Philadelphia Police Department and filled out visa applications through the State Department website.

As some researchers also warn of potentially catastrophic risks from AI, regulators and lawmakers are grappling with increasing urgency on how to keep the technology in check, including through existing statutes.

“There is a whole set of laws and regulations that deal with kind of what you’re describing, the bad actor scenario,” Scott Kupor, director of the Office of Personnel Management and a vice chair of Trump’s SI Force, told CNN last week.

Trump argued last month that only a “strong and smart” president is needed for AI safety, writing in a Truth Social post that the U.S. already has “tremendous criminal and regulatory power” over AI firms.

FTC Chair Andrew Ferguson, who serves as one of the task force’s vice-chairs, is already utilizing the agency’s consumer protection authority.

The agency opened an investigation earlier this year into AI firms OpenAI and Anthropic over the potential dangers their models pose to consumers. It sent the two companies civil subpoenas, just days after Anthropic disclosed the false homicide tip.

“This is an area tailor-made for the FTC,” said William Kovacic, who served as a commissioner from 2006 to 2011 and chaired the agency for a year.

“If we rely on existing law, the FTC’s probably got the best tools,” he told The Hill. “And if we create new laws, they ought to be given to the FTC.”

Under the law, the agency is tasked with preventing unfair methods of competition, as well as unfair or deceptive acts or practices. This could include knowingly selling products with serious potential defects or knowingly failing to adopt proper safeguards, Kovacic said.

He pointed to an instance where an AI agent “takes a hike and does malicious things,” and the developers knew this was a possibility but didn’t warn users.

“These go to the real sources of anxiety that people have about AI, that it’s going to be like the sorcerer’s apprentice, where the magician sets in motion a series of events that the magician ultimately does not control,” he added.

Other tech law experts acknowledge the power of existing laws, but they left the door open to exploring new laws to address the most unique qualities of AI.

Jennifer Huddleston, a senior tech policy fellow at the libertarian think tank Cato Institute, called existing laws a “good first step” but said “there also needs to be conversations” asking, “are there areas that are truly novel that are not covered, or where existing law can’t keep up?”

This could include the use of copyrighted work in the AI era, or non-consensual images made or enhanced with AI, she said.

Sharma said existing law has “real force here” but believes the current laws are still not sufficient for what she thinks “should be accomplished with a legal regime” on AI.

Laws, Sharma suggested, may not be ready to address emotional, psychological or cognitive harms. She pointed to instances in which criminals allegedly use AI chatbots to plan out an illegal act or harm to others.

In Canada, the family of a girl critically wounded in a school shooting sued OpenAI , alleging it was aware of the suspect’s planned shooting due to his chat logs but failed to alert authorities.

“Historically, descriptively, we’ve seen that when there is kind of a watershed moment in innovation, where we have a new technology, a new product, it’s interacting with the world in a new way,” Sharma said.

“We’ve often found that the status quo of the law isn’t enough because it wasn’t built and developed over time in a way that anticipated this new world order,” she added.

Gabriel Weil, a non-resident senior fellow at the Institute for Law and AI, said AI companies could also face negligence or product liability lawsuits over their products. But he underscored that “litigation’s pretty slow.”

“Courts have to wait for the right case to come around,” he said. “They can’t just announce their policies in advance. And the litigation working its way through the appeals courts can take years. And AI development, as you may have noticed, is moving quite fast.”

If the goal is to shape behavior with liability expectations, Weil said, “you would want the expectations to be clear very soon.” He argued the slow timeline of litigation “would behoove Congress to get out in front of this or state legislatures.”

He suggested lawmakers should establish new liability rules for AI, holding companies responsible when their AI agents engage in harmful conduct that a human could be sued over. This is the premise of the CLAIM Act, recently introduced by Rep. Lori Trahan (D-Mass.), which Weil helped draft.

But the Trump administration’s reliance on current law undercuts the growing push in Congress to codify new laws to hold tech companies liable, as Republican leaders defer to the president and his preference for a hands-off approach to AI regulation.

While the federal government has scrambled to address the technology’s risks, state legislatures and attorneys general have been charging ahead with efforts to hold companies accountable.

In a first-of-its-kind lawsuit , Florida sued OpenAI and its CEO Sam Altman, alleging the company promoted a product they knew could harm users. Florida Attorney General James Uthmeier (R) also alleged Altman is personally liable for harm to state residents.

And last week, eight states sued OpenAI for allegedly misleading users over the safety of its chatbots.

“You have some kinds of claims that could be consistent across both [state and federal] but a lot of the activity that’s happening is happening at the state level,” Sharma said. “A lot of this is not happening at the federal government’s behest.”
